author: fester
body: A literal pattern's value arrives as its source spelling. `True` and `False` are the Boolean scrutinee's 1 and 0; `parse-int-text` reads neither and answers 0 for both, so every `is True` and `is False` compared against 0 and the arms inverted. Characters were reduced to digits by the desugarer and pass through unchanged. This mirrors the compiler's `pat-lit-to-integer`.

author: fester
body: A literal sub-pattern inside a constructor pattern used to be DROPPED: this walk bound IrVarPat and let everything else fall out of its otherwise arm, so the constructor tag was the only thing tested and `is BInt (0)` matched any BInt. Whichever arm's CONSTRUCTOR matched first won, which collapses a multi-way dispatch onto one arm. Measured on ARM64 2026-07-21 with codex/test/literal-subpattern: by-int answered 10 for every input, by-text 20, by-flag 30, by-pair 40. The x86-64 emitter carried the identical defect until 2026-07-20, where it made apps/cvmm's Calculator treat every operator as plus.

author: fester
body: Each literal now emits its own test and its own branch, and every index this returns has to be patched by the caller -- a single patch slot was the other half of the original bug, because a second failing test had nowhere to go.

author: fester
body: A Text literal cannot be a cmp. The scrutinee holds a POINTER and a64-pat-lit-to-integer answers a number for the spelling, so `is "sin"` matched nothing at any nesting depth. Text goes through __str_eq, the helper IrEq already uses for the same comparison.

author: fester
body: `opening` is declined by name for the reason the LIR try declines it: the framed path is not an ordinary emitter for the entry point, it appends the print-result epilogue (`integer-to-text` then `print-line-uni`), and the frameless path has no such special case. The old gate excluded `opening` only incidentally -- it is never self-recursive, so `a64-should-tco` was False -- and the widening to plain leaves would otherwise admit `opening : Integer = 0` frameless and emit a correct function that prints nothing. `list-append-perf-N8-L7` caught exactly that.

author: fester
body: The second analysis is a POSITIVE whitelist, and it is positive on purpose: the reverted attempt used a blocklist of call shapes and was defeated by every shape it forgot to list. A frameless leaf writes no frame, so its body may emit no `bl` (a `bl` overwrites x30 with no save and the `ret` re-enters the body forever) and may touch no local past the six-register frameless file. Rather than enumerate the emitting shapes -- a bare nullary name (`f (x) = x + some-constant`), a list literal (`aes-sbox`, `cpt-key`), a record, a match, an act, and whatever the emitter grows next, each an `a64-emit-call-to` -- this walk names the shapes that are SAFE and frames everything else. A body is safe iff it is a bound name, a literal, a negate of a safe body, a non-appending binary over safe operands, a let whose value and body are safe, an if whose parts are safe, or an application of an `a64-is-inline-here` builtin to safe arguments. Any other node -- any call to a non-inline name, any allocating literal -- is unsafe, so the default arm frames. Coverage given up on purpose: a leaf that reads a bare nullary constant or builds a small record stays framed. The win is the thousands of pure arithmetic and bitwise leaves, which this admits and the old TCO-only gate did not. `codex/test/frameless-leaf-probe` pins the shapes.

author: fester
body: The whitelist was arrived at by shipping a blocklist first and watching it regress `chacha20poly1305`, `aesgcm256` and `cce-tier1` -- all green on the base, all broken by a frameless table constant the blocklist did not name. A blocklist for this is a list of every way a body can emit a call, which is not a closed set; a whitelist of the ways it cannot is.

author: fester
body: The frameless analysis treats every `a64-is-known-inline` name as call-free, but that list is BROADER than the set `a64-is-inline-here` actually inlines: `abs`, `negate`, `min` and `max` are analysed as inline yet, when a definition in the module shadows one, the dispatch emits a REAL `bl` to it (user-wins, deliberately kept for these -- a shadowed `abs` answers the user's body on x86-64 and must here too). A `bl` in a frameless function clobbers x30 with no save, and the `ret` returns into the loop body forever. So a body that calls a shadowed member of that residue takes the framed path, where the `bl` is what a frame is for. The bit ops and mods are NOT in the residue: `a64-is-inline-here` inlines them regardless of registration, so the emission agrees with the analysis there and frameless coverage is unchanged for them.

author: fester
body: Writing a parameter destroys the value any later argument still reads out of it, so the two writes have an order and only one of them may be wrong. If argument 0 reads parameter 1, parameter 0 must be written first; if argument 1 reads parameter 0, parameter 1 must be written first. Both at once is a cycle and no order saves it, so that alone falls back to the general path, which saves every argument before copying any.

author: fester
body: p-shift (n) (a) = p-shift (n - 1) (a + a - n) is the shape that exposed this: it answered -2 where -33 is correct, because a + a - n was evaluated against the already-decremented n. The guard tested only the safe direction, so the hazard it existed to catch was the one it let through. RiscVCodeGen3's rv-emit-tail-call-direct is the same rule.

author: fester
body: A handle saves each operation's current handler for the duration of its body and puts it back afterwards. That saving used to PUSH on the stack, and a spill slot is addressed off SP (a64-store-local: [SP, slot*8 + 96]), so a body that spilled resolved every slot 16 bytes per clause away from where the same slot resolves outside the handle. Two handles in sequence then aliased: measured, a two-clause handle wrote its result to SP+128 after popping and the next handle wrote SP+160 while SP was still 32 low -- the same byte -- so the earlier result came back holding the later one. The saved handlers live in ordinary frame locals now and SP does not move inside a frame.

author: fester
body: Name resolution: first match among the DEFINITIONS, with a leading runtime registration skipped when a definition exists. The fourth parameter is the runtime/definition boundary -- the count of names the runtime registered before the first definition was emitted, stamped into `extra.runtime-funcs` by `a64-emit-module` -- and the rule is exactly two cases. A name whose first occurrence is at or past the boundary is a definition, and the FIRST definition wins, which is what the tree has always done and what `dtls-hello`'s expectations encode for its colliding hello builders. A name whose first occurrence is below the boundary is a runtime helper; if a definition of the same name exists above the boundary, the definition wins -- that is shadowing (`codex/test/shadow-builtin-fold`: `text-length (s) = 99` must beat the runtime's `text-length`) -- and otherwise the helper is the only thing there is. Plain last-match was tried first and bound `dtls-hello`'s duplicate definitions to the wrong body; measured both ways 2026-07-23. A caller passing 0 gets plain first-match.
